heading: Languages Yon runs
body:
Yon supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, PHP, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua directly. Each controller can also use provider annotations (annotations on the classes that other classes need). Tachyon turns all annotations into plain code before the route runs. Tachyon starts each process and adapts the protocol. You need no annotation package at run time. To call a class in another of these languages, declare a `@Gateway` method. To reach other programs, call `relay(command, request)` yourself, or name the program in a `@Gateway` command. The list below shows the program that runs each language. `ty doctor` checks that these programs are installed. A Rust handler builds with Cargo and the `http` crate, offline first. A Dart handler needs the `shelf` package in the pub cache, or the network, because Tachyon runs `dart pub get`.

Groovy (ADR 0072) writes the annotations as Java does: `@RequestRoute('/orders')`, `@GetRoute`, `@Service`, `@Needs`. Tachyon reads Groovy with the Java rules, and a semicolon at the end of a line is optional. Every field and method has a declared type, such as `String name` or `List<Order> findOrders()`; a member declared with `def` stops the build (TY1334), and a local variable inside a method may still use `def`. A model is a record, an enum or a class with typed fields, and code reads it with `import models.Order`. Groovy uses the Java protocol runtime, so the request is `HttpExchange` and `Yon.relay(command, exchange)` works as in Java. Tachyon compiles your Groovy together with that Java runtime (joint compilation) into one jar with the Groovy core library and runs it on the JDK. Tachyon finds Groovy 4 or newer through `GROOVY_HOME` or `groovyc` on `PATH`. Two Groovy rules matter for Tachyon code: `1.5` is a `BigDecimal`, so write `1.5d` for a `double`, and a closure that you put into a map needs its type, such as `{ request, execution -> ... } as Behaviors.HttpAdapter`. Groovy also reads a single map argument to a record constructor as named arguments, so write `new CatalogSummary(summary: summary)`.

F# (ADR 0073) writes the annotations as F# attributes, each on its own line: `[<RequestRoute("/orders")>]`, `[<GetRoute>]`, `[<Service>]`. A type takes the roles it needs as the parameters of its primary constructor, `type OrderService(orderStore: OrderStore) =`, the way Spring injects a class with one constructor. This is the recommended form. A settable property with `[<Needs>]` receives a role too, like a Spring field: `[<Needs>] member val OrderStore : OrderStore = Unchecked.defaultof<OrderStore> with get, set`, and `[<Named("...")>]` chooses another provider. Members that Tachyon reads write their types, for example `member this.GetOrder(id: int64) : Order =`. A model is an F# record, and code reads it with `open Models`. An F# file holds one type and no `module` or `namespace` line, and it has no file-level `let` (TY1335). F# runs on .NET with the same protocol runtime as C#, so F# code uses `Yon.Relay`, `DataSource`, `HttpRequestMessage` and `HttpResponseMessage` as C# does. Behavior annotations work in F# through the C# behavior runtime: a member whose body Tachyon writes, such as a query or a Convert method, is an F# `abstract` member, and the behavior context is a `behaviors` member of the class. Events and lifecycle hooks work as in C#, and a class takes its ApplicationEventPublisher as a primary constructor parameter. F# controllers hold SocketRoute and StreamRoute as C# does: a socket member takes the SocketSession, and a stream member returns `seq<'T>` or `IAsyncEnumerable<'T>`. An F# TestSetup declares `static member configure`, as in C#, and each case of an F# test unit reads its behavior context as `this.behaviors`. ty test counts the F# members that a case really called.

Lua (ADR 0085) has no annotation syntax, so an annotation is a comment on its own line: `-- @RequestRoute("/orders")`, `-- @GetRoute`, `-- @Service`, `-- @Needs`. Lua ignores the comment, so the file runs unchanged. A Lua class is one global table in its own file, `OrderService = {}`, and its methods are `function OrderService:list()`. The fields of the class sit in the table, one field on each line, such as `order_service = nil,` under `-- @Needs`. Types are LuaCATS comments, which the Lua language server also reads: `---@param id integer`, `---@return Order[]`, `---@type OrderService`, and a model is a `---@class` with `---@field` lines. `local Name = {}`, `return Name`, `require`, a second table or code outside a method stops the build (TY1357), because Tachyon joins the class files of one realm into one program. A route parameter without a marker and root middleware receive a request table with `method`, `path`, `headers` and `body`, and middleware answers with a `{ status, headers, body }` list. An error is a table whose metatable is its error type, `error(setmetatable({ message = "order 42" }, OrderNotFound))`. Tachyon runs Lua 5.4 or newer with the `lua` program. Events and lifecycle hooks work in Lua: `-- @OnStart`, `-- @OnStop`, `-- @OnEvent` and `-- @Order` above a method, and an event is a model table that `ApplicationEventPublisher:publish_event(value)` publishes. Behavior annotations work in Lua too. A class opens its context with `self.behaviors = Behaviors.create(Setup, { partition = "orders", signal = BehaviorSignal.new() })`. Tachyon wraps each behavior method, such as a `-- @Cached` or `-- @Retry({...})` method. A Lua `-- @StreamRoute` method sends each value with `coroutine.yield(value)`, and a `-- @SocketRoute` class gets a session with `session:send(message)` and `session:open_sessions()`. A model marked `-- @Topic` is a topic: a Lua route publishes it and a Lua `-- @OnEvent` method hears it from other languages. `@InBackground` is not available in Lua yet: a Lua file that uses it stops the build with `TY1308` (the annotation is not available in Lua). Resources are not available in Lua either: a Lua class that needs `DataSource` or `RedisTemplate`, calls `relay`, or declares `@HTTPClient` or `@Gateway` stops the build and names the resource. A Lua model cannot carry `Settings`, `Setting` or `Checked` yet (`TY1310`, ADR 0092), and a Lua `Store` is not yet a provider that another class can inject (`TY2015`). Lua is also a Tac language: a page service written as a Lua class table runs on Tachyon's Lua WebAssembly runtime. ty test counts the Lua methods that a case really called, in both realms.

Go (ADR 0045) writes each annotation as a `// @Name` comment on its own line, and its files use `package main`. Your own Go packages and vendored third-party modules live in the Go module in `server/packages/` (ADR 0095). A Go `// @StreamRoute` method returns `iter.Seq[Model]`, or `iter.Seq2[Model, error]` when the stream can fail, and a method that takes the `*http.Request` reads the time limit from `request.Context()`. A Rust `#[OnEvent]` listener may carry `#[InBackground]`: it stays synchronous and runs after the other listeners of the event.
